entries.lesson_core_move: Apply the sifting property to convert an integral of a continuous-time signal multiplied by a shifted unit impulse into the signal value sampled at the impulse location.

sections.section_title: Introduction to The Sifting Property

blocks.text: When you see $x(\tau)\,\delta(\tau-t_0)$ inside an integral, read the shifted impulse as a sampling cue. It marks the one time that survives, $\tau=t_0$, and tells you to keep the value of $x(\tau)$ there.
The clean base case is the impulse at the origin. If the center is $\tau=0$, the integral returns the signal value at $0$.
The shifted version keeps the same rule. Moving the impulse center from $0$ to $t_0$ moves the sampled value with it.

So the sifting property is a substitution pattern, not a rule for integrating $x(\tau)$ term by term. Identify the impulse location, substitute that time into $x(\tau)$, and write the sampled result directly as $x(t_0)$.

sections.section_title: Sifting a Signal with an Impulse at the Origin

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the origin-centered impulse $\delta(\tau)$, so this is a sampling problem at $\tau=0$. By the sifting property, the impulse keeps only the signal value at the origin.
Here $x(\tau)=\tau^2+4\tau+1$, so the sample at the origin is found by substituting $\tau=0$ into the signal expression.
So the integral evaluates to $1$. The impulse does not make you integrate the polynomial term by term; it makes you read off the sampled value at the impulse location.

sections.section_title: Sifting a Signal with a Shifted Impulse

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the shifted impulse $\delta(\tau-1.5)$, so the sample point is $t_0=1.5$. By the sifting property, the integral keeps only the value of the signal at that time.
Here $x(\tau)=\cos\tau+2$, so substitute $\tau=1.5$ into the signal expression.
So the integral evaluates to $\cos(1.5)+2$. The shift in the impulse simply moves the sampling location from $0$ to $1.5$.

sections.section_title: Sifting a Time-Domain Formula at the Impulse Location

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the shifted impulse $\delta(\tau+1)$, which is the same as $\delta(\tau-(-1))$. So the sample point is $t_0=-1$.
Here $x(\tau)=\tau^3+\tau-\frac{1}{\tau}$, so substitute $\tau=-1$ into the signal expression.
So the integral evaluates to $-1$. The shifted impulse simply moves the sampling location from $0$ to $-1$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Evaluate integrals containing shifted unit impulses by checking whether the impulse time lies inside the integration limits and substituting the sampled value when it does.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Evaluating Integrals with Shifted Impulses

blocks.text: A shifted impulse $\delta(\tau-t_0)$ tells you where to sample the signal inside the integral. The key cue is the impulse location $t_0$, because that is the only time value the impulse preserves.

For a finite interval, first check whether the impulse time lies inside the limits $[a,b]$. If $t_0\in[a,b]$, the integral returns the sample $x(t_0)$; if $t_0$ is outside the interval, the impulse contributes $0$.

blocks.latex: \int_a^b x(\tau)\,\delta(\tau-t_0)\,d\tau = \begin{cases}x(t_0), & a\le t_0\le b \\ 0, & t_0<a \text{ or } t_0>b\end{cases}

blocks.text: So the procedure is simple: read the impulse center first, test it against the integration limits, and then substitute that time into $x(\tau)$ only when the impulse sits inside the interval. If more than one shifted impulse appears later, apply the same rule term by term.

sections.section_title: Evaluating an Integral When the Impulse Time Is Inside the Limits

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the shifted impulse at $\tau=1$, and $1$ lies inside the integration limits $[-2,5]$. That means the inside-case rule applies: sample the signal at the impulse time instead of integrating the signal normally.
Here the signal factor is $x(\tau)=3\tau$, so the rule gives $x(1)$. The impulse does not change the signal shape; it only selects the value at the impulse location.
So the integral evaluates to $3$. The same one-line substitution is the whole move when the impulse time is inside the limits.

sections.section_title: Evaluating an Integral When the Impulse Time Is Outside the Limits

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the shifted impulse at $\tau=3$, with $x(\tau)=\cos(\tau)$. The interval test is the only decision here: $3$ is not in $[-2,1]$, so the impulse sits outside the integration window.
When the impulse time is outside the limits, there is no sampled value to return, so the integral is zero.
That is the entire outside-case branch: check the limits first, then return $0$ if the impulse location is not included.

sections.section_title: Evaluating Integrals with Multiple Shifted Impulses

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is linearity: split the expression into separate shifted-impulse terms and test each impulse time against the same limits $[-2,3]$. The impulse times are $1$, $-4$, and $4$, so only the first term lies inside the interval.

The inside term samples its paired signal factor at $\tau=1$, so $\int_{-2}^{3} (\tau+2)\,\delta(\tau-1)d\tau = 1+2 = 3$. The other two terms contribute $0$ because their impulses are outside the interval.
So the whole expression evaluates to $3$. The rule is still the same one impulse at a time: check the bounds, sample the inside terms, and drop the outside terms.

entries.lesson_core_move: Rewrite impulses with nonstandard arguments as scaled shifted impulses by locating each argument zero and applying the correct inverse-slope weight.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Impulses with Nonstandard Arguments

blocks.text: When an impulse is written as $\delta(g(t))$ instead of the standard shifted form $\delta(t-t_0)$, the job is to find where the argument is zero and rewrite the result as a shifted standard impulse. That zero tells you the impulse location, and the local slope tells you the scaling factor.

For a pure scale, the impulse stays centered at $t=0$, but the argument is compressed or stretched by the factor $a$. The coefficient must therefore be $1/|a|$ so the impulse keeps unit area whether $a$ is positive or negative.

For a shifted linear argument, solve $at-b=0$ to locate the impulse at $t=\frac{b}{a}$, then attach the same inverse-slope weight from the factor that vanishes there. When the argument later factors into several simple linear terms, apply the same idea at each zero and add the resulting shifted impulses.

sections.section_title: Rewriting an Impulse with a Pure Time Scale

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is a pure time scale: the argument is $4t$, so the impulse is still centered at $t=0$. Match it to the template $\delta(at)$ and use the inverse-magnitude of the scale factor.
Here $a=4$, so $|a|=4$ and the coefficient is $\frac{1}{4}$. The standard-form rewrite is $\delta(4t)=\frac{1}{4}\delta(t)$.

sections.section_title: Rewriting an Impulse with a Shifted Linear Argument

example_content.example_prompt: Rewrite $\delta(3t-6)$ as a sum of weighted shifted impulses.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a shifted linear argument, so match $3t-6$ to the template $at-b$. Solve the argument zero first: $3t-6=0$ gives $t=2$.
Here $a=3$, so the inverse-slope weight is $1/|a|=1/3$. With the zero at $t=2$, the standard-form impulse is $\frac{1}{3}\delta(t-2)$.

sections.section_title: Rewriting an Impulse with a Negative Slope

example_content.example_prompt: Rewrite $\delta(-2t+6)$ as a weighted shifted standard impulse.

explanation_blocks.text: This still matches the linear template $at-b$, but now the slope is negative: $a=-2$. Solve the zero first: $-2t+6=0$ gives $t=3$.
The negative sign changes how you locate the root, but the impulse weight uses $|a|$. So the coefficient is $1/2$, not $-1/2$, and the shifted impulse is centered at $t=3$.

sections.section_title: Rewriting an Impulse Argument with Multiple Simple Zeros

example_content.example_prompt: Rewrite $\delta((t-1)(t+2))$ as a sum of shifted impulses.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a product with two simple zeros, so treat the argument as $f(t)$ and use the multi-root rule $\delta(f(t))=\sum_k \frac{1}{|f'(t_k)|}\delta(t-t_k)$. Here $f(t)=(t-1)(t+2)$, so the zeros are $t=1$ and $t=-2$.
Each zero contributes one shifted impulse with its own inverse-slope weight. Since both derivative magnitudes are $3$, each term gets coefficient $1/3$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Apply change-of-variables reasoning to evaluate impulse integrals by transforming the impulse argument, adjusting the scale factor, and preserving the correct sampled time.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Change of Variables with Impulses

blocks.text: Start with the unit-slope sifting pattern: if the impulse is already written as $\delta(t-t_0)$, then $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)\,\delta(t-t_0)\,dt=x(t_0)$. That is the standard form the later algebra must recover.

For a linear impulse argument $\delta(a t-b)$, first find the zero of the argument by solving $a t-b=0$. The sampled time is $t_0=b/a$, and the change of variables must preserve that time while turning the impulse into standard form.
Use the simplest nonunit case, $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)\,\delta(2t-4)\,dt$. Set $u=2t-4$, so $dt=du/2$, and rewrite the integral so the impulse becomes $\delta(u)$.
That same change-of-variables step gives the general positive-slope rule: the root $t_0=b/a$ is the sample point, and the slope contributes the inverse factor $1/|a|$.

Negative slope does not change the sampled time; it only changes the algebra of the substitution, which is why the absolute value appears. The rule to carry forward is simple: find the zero, convert to unit-impulse form, divide by the slope magnitude, and evaluate the signal at that sampled time.

sections.section_title: Converting a Positive Linear Impulse Argument

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the linear impulse argument $4t-8$. Find its zero first: $4t-8=0$ gives $t=2$. That is the sampled time the change of variables must preserve.
Use the substitution $u=4t-8$, so $dt=du/4$. Then rewrite the integral so the impulse is in standard form $\delta(u)$ and the signal is evaluated at the transformed time.
So the positive-slope linear impulse argument contributes the scale factor $1/4$, and the signal is sampled at the root $t=2$. The worked result is $\frac{1}{4}y(2)$.

sections.section_title: Evaluating the Signal Factor After the Variable Change

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the linear impulse argument $5t-10$. Solve $5t-10=0$ to get the sampled time $t=2$; that is the time the signal factor must be evaluated after the change of variables.
Use $u=5t-10$, so $dt=du/5$ and $t=(u+10)/5$. Because the signal factor is $t^2+1$, replace $t$ inside that factor before sifting.
So the slope contributes the factor $1/5$, and the transformed signal is sampled at the root $t=2$. The worked result is $1$.

sections.section_title: Converting a Negative Linear Impulse Argument

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the negative-slope impulse argument $-3t+9$. Solve $-3t+9=0$ to get the sampled time $t=3$; the sign of the slope does not change the sample point.
Use $u=-3t+9$, so $dt=-du/3$ and $t=(9-u)/3$. The minus sign in $dt$ is the sign bookkeeping that will turn into the absolute scale factor.
So the negative slope still gives a positive factor $1/3$, and the signal is sampled at the same root $t=3$. The worked result is $\frac{1}{3}x(3)$.

sections.section_title: Checking Definite Integral Bounds After the Variable Change

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $\int_{0}^{2}x(t)\,\delta(4t-2)\,dt$ and explain why the bounds matter.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the sampled time from $4t-2=0$. Solve first: $t_0=1/2$. Because $1/2$ lies inside the interval $[0,2]$, the impulse contributes; if the sampled time were outside the interval, the definite integral would be $0$.
Use $u=4t-2$, so $dt=du/4$ and $t=(u+2)/4$. The finite bounds move with the substitution, but the $\delta$ still samples only when the transformed interval contains $u=0$.
So the bounds act as an inclusion check: here $t_0=1/2$ is inside $[0,2]$, so the scaled result is $\frac{1}{4}x(1/2)$. If the sampled time missed the interval, the answer would be $0$.

entries.lesson_title: Unit Step as the Integral of an Impulse
entries.lesson_core_move: Convert the accumulated integral of a shifted unit impulse into a shifted unit step by identifying when the impulse area has been included.

sections.lesson_title: Unit Step as the Integral of an Impulse
sections.section_title: Introduction to Unit Step as the Integral of an Impulse

blocks.text: Let $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}\delta(\tau)\,d\tau$. This is an accumulation problem: it counts how much of the unit impulse's area has been included as the upper limit moves past $\tau=0$.
Before the limit reaches the impulse, nothing has been accumulated, so $y(t)=0$ for $t<0$. Once the limit reaches or passes the impulse, the full unit area is included, so $y(t)=1$ for $t\ge 0$.

That $0$-to-$1$ switch is exactly the unit step $u(t)$, so the accumulated impulse is written as $y(t)=u(t)$. Read this as the basic switch rule: off before $0$, on at and after $0$, with the matching reverse relation $\frac{d}{dt}u(t)=\delta(t)$.
Use this as the base case for shifted impulses later: the only thing that changes is the time at which the accumulation window first includes the impulse area.

sections.lesson_title: Unit Step as the Integral of an Impulse
sections.section_title: Accumulating an Unshifted Unit Impulse

example_content.example_prompt: Evaluate $\int_{-\infty}^{t} \delta(\tau)\,d\tau$ and write the result as a unit-step expression.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the unit impulse at the origin. Let $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}\delta(\tau)\,d\tau$, so the task is to decide when the moving upper limit has included the unit area of $\delta(\tau)$.

For $t<0$, the interval $(-\infty,t]$ stops before $\tau=0$, so no impulse area has been included and $y(t)=0$. For $t\ge 0$, the interval includes the impulse, so the full unit area has been included and $y(t)=1$.
So the accumulated impulse is exactly the unit step: $y(t)=u(t)$. This is the baseline unshifted case that later examples will shift to other impulse locations.

sections.lesson_title: Unit Step as the Integral of an Impulse
sections.section_title: Accumulating a Shifted Unit Impulse

example_content.example_prompt: Find $\int_{-\infty}^{t}\delta(\tau-3)\,d\tau$ and express the result as a unit step.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the shifted unit impulse at $\tau=3$. Let $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}\delta(\tau-3)\,d\tau$, so the task is to decide when the moving upper limit has included the impulse area at that shift point.

For $t<3$, the interval $(-\infty,t]$ stops before $\tau=3$, so no impulse area has been included and $y(t)=0$. For $t\ge 3$, the interval includes the impulse, so the full unit area has been included and $y(t)=1$.

So the accumulated shifted impulse is exactly the shifted unit step: $y(t)=u(t-3)$. The only thing that changed from the unshifted case is the time at which the accumulation window first includes the unit area.

sections.lesson_title: Unit Step as the Integral of an Impulse
sections.section_title: Deciding Whether the Impulse Has Been Included

example_content.example_prompt: Decide if the impulse at $\tau=2$ has been accumulated in $\int_{-\infty}^{t}\delta(\tau-2)\,d\tau$ for $t=-1,2,5$ and state the matching step form.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the shifted unit impulse centered at $\tau=2$. Let $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}\delta(\tau-2)\,d\tau$, so the task is to test whether the moving upper limit has reached the shift point before labeling the output.

For $t=-1$, the interval $(-\infty,t]$ stops before $\tau=2$, so the impulse has not been included and the value is $0$. For $t=2$, the interval reaches the impulse location, so the unit area is included and the value is $1$. For $t=5$, the interval is already past the impulse, so the value is still $1$.

So the inclusion test switches exactly at $t=2$, which means the accumulated impulse is the shifted unit step $u(t-2)$. The rule to carry forward is to compare the moving upper limit to the impulse location, then write $0$ before inclusion and $1$ at or after inclusion.

sections.lesson_title: Unit Step as the Integral of an Impulse
sections.section_title: Converting Scaled Impulse Accumulations into Scaled Steps

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a scaled impulse centered at $\tau=-1$. Use linearity first: the factor $5$ stays attached while the accumulation test still checks whether the moving upper limit has reached the impulse location.

For $t<-1$, the interval $(-\infty,t]$ stops before $\tau=-1$, so the impulse has not been included and the value is $0$. For $t\ge -1$, the interval includes the full unit area, so the scale factor carries through and the value is $5$.
So the accumulated scaled impulse is $y(t)=5u(t+1)$. The rule to carry forward is simple: keep the coefficient, check the shifted include point, and then write the corresponding scaled step.

entries.lesson_title: Unit Impulse as the Derivative of a Unit Step
entries.lesson_core_move: Differentiate a shifted unit step to convert its instantaneous jump into the corresponding shifted unit impulse.

sections.lesson_title: Unit Impulse as the Derivative of a Unit Step
sections.section_title: Introduction to Unit Impulse as the Derivative of a Unit Step

blocks.text: A derivative is the right tool when a signal has an abrupt jump. For a unit step $u(t)$, that jump happens at the switching time, so the derivative is represented by a unit impulse at the same location.

Start with the base case. Differentiate the unshifted step $u(t)$ and read the result as the origin impulse $\delta(t)$. This is the identity to remember when a step transition becomes an impulse form.

The same reading rule applies after a shift. If the step is $u(t-t_0)$, the jump occurs at $t=t_0$, so the impulse moves to the same time. In practice, you locate the impulse by reading the step argument.

A constant scale factor passes straight through by linearity, so the weighted shifted step $A\,u(t-t_0)$ differentiates to $A\,\delta(t-t_0)$. That is the compact form you will reuse in later examples: keep the same shift, keep the same scale, and replace the jump with an impulse.

sections.lesson_title: Unit Impulse as the Derivative of a Unit Step
sections.section_title: Differentiating the Basic Unit Step

explanation_blocks.text: Differentiate the basic unit step $u(t)$. The cue is the jump at $t=0$, so we apply the tutorial rule that a step transition differentiates to an impulse at the same location.
Because the step is flat everywhere except at the jump, the derivative is zero away from $t=0$ and concentrated entirely at the origin. The result is the unit impulse $\delta(t)$ with unit weight.

sections.lesson_title: Unit Impulse as the Derivative of a Unit Step
sections.section_title: Differentiating a Shifted Unit Step

explanation_blocks.text: Differentiate the shifted step $u(t-3)$. The cue is the jump at $t=3$, so we use the same rule as before: a step transition differentiates to an impulse at its switch time.
The shift stays in the impulse location, so the result is centered at $t=3$ instead of at the origin. The final answer is the unit impulse $\delta(t-3)$ with unit weight.

sections.lesson_title: Unit Impulse as the Derivative of a Unit Step
sections.section_title: Differentiating a Scaled Shifted Unit Step

explanation_blocks.text: Differentiate the scaled shifted step $5u(t-2)$. The cue is the jump at $t=2$, and the factor $5$ is a constant gain, so we pull it outside the derivative before applying the step rule.

The shift stays with the impulse, so the result is centered at $t=2$. Reattaching the constant gain gives the final answer $5\delta(t-2)$, with the factor multiplying the impulse and not the argument.

sections.lesson_title: Unit Impulse as the Derivative of a Unit Step
sections.section_title: Differentiating Sums of Shifted Unit Steps

explanation_blocks.text: Differentiate the sum of shifted steps term by term. The cue is the three separate jump times at $t=1$, $t=-2$, and $t=4$, so each step becomes an impulse at its own switch location.

Now apply the shifted-step rule to each term and keep the coefficients attached to their own impulses. The linearity of differentiation lets you preserve the order of the terms while converting each jump into the matching impulse.
The result is a sum of shifted impulses, one for each step in the original expression. Each impulse stays at the same switch time as its step, and each coefficient stays with the term it came from.
